rv.q: Jonas has crafted a thoughtful, truthful meditation on parenthood, community, and the stories we tell to survive.
A Woman Among Women swims through puzzling experimental choices before it lands with a bang.
It all feels so unlike a conventional musical score that the audience somehow knows not to applaud them.
A Woman Among Women, though, frustrates more than excites.
A terribly talky, at times even tedious, theater exercise that fails to engage pity or any emotion other than occasional confusion.
And while I applaud the effort, the work falls well short of its ambitions.

One way to grapple with the mostly white, mostly male classics of American drama is to rethink them entirely, from a female point of view. That’s the mission of Julia May Jonas in a A Woman Among Women, an updated spin on Arthur Miller’s All My Sons built around the well-respected founder of a women’s wellness center.
Frustratingly slow to ignite, but genuinely thought-provoking once it does

A Woman Among Women is a mixed bag, with acerbic humor, disturbing situations, and a final reckoning that shakes the community to its core, infused with musical numbers that lengthen the show and break the mood and narrative flow with little reason.

cn.t: Jonas's feminist reimagining of "All My Sons" offers an intriguing premise and strong lead performance, but critics find the execution uneven, with a slow first two-thirds that dwells too long before reaching its more compelling moral revelations.
